The eyestripe surgeonfish Acanthurus dussumieri is a widespread Indo-Pacific herbivore that attains a maximum recorded total length of 54 centimeters [Li = 54 centimeters], a value derived from extensive field surveys across the greater coral reef systems of the region. This ultimate length is considerably larger than that reported for several smaller-bodied congeners, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritises continued somatic expansion throughout the early adult years. In this species, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was approximately 9% [GSI = approximately 9%] when measured under stable thermal conditions of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C].

The initiation of reproductive activity in Acanthurus dussumieri occurs once individuals attain a total length of approximately 25 centimeters [Lp = approximately 25 centimeters], marking the onset of puberty. This size threshold corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of roughly 389 g [Wwp = roughly 389 g]rams, which was estimated using established length-weight conversion parameters derived from morphometric analyses of conspecific populations. Achieving this body size typically requires several years of sustained growth on the reef, during which the fish must accumulate sufficient lipid reserves to support the energetic demands of gametogenesis. The shift from a purely somatic growth trajectory to one that incorporates gonadal development represents a fundamental transition in the life cycle, and the specific length at which it occurs has important implications for management; if fishing removes individuals before they reach 25 cm [Lp = 25 cm], the spawning stock may be progressively depleted. Field observations suggest that this pubertal length is relatively conservative across the species range, though local environmental conditions such as food availability and density-dependent competition can modulate the exact timing.

At the earliest stage of life, following egg fertilisation and embryonic development within the pelagic environment, newly hatched larvae of the eyestripe surgeonfish emerge at an exceedingly small size. The estimated wet weight at birth is 0.00018 g [Wwb = 0.00018 g]rams, a value derived from the typical egg diameter of 0.7 millimeters documented in the closely related species Acanthurus lineatus and the geometric relationship describing a sphere. This minuscule initial mass represents a profound challenge for the yolk-sac larva, which must rely on endogenous yolk reserves during the lecithotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding. The duration of this non-feeding interval is critically dependent upon water temperature, and under the typical thermal regime of the tropical Indo-Pacific, the yolk is absorbed rapidly, forcing the prolarva to locate and capture suitable planktonic prey within a narrow window or face starvation. This extreme vulnerability at birth is partially offset by high fecundity, as females release large numbers of pelagic eggs during each spawning event, ensuring that at least a fraction of the cohort survives the perilous larval period to recruit onto the reef.

As individuals approach the asymptotic body size characteristic of the species, the ultimate wet weight is calculated to be approximately 3743 g [Wwi = approximately 3743 g]rams, a value that corresponds to the 54-centimeter maximum total length through the scaling relationship typical for acanthurids. This substantial adult mass distinguishes Acanthurus dussumieri from many of its smaller congeners and places it among the larger-bodied surgeonfish species within the genus. The transition from the pubertal weight of 389 g [Wwp = 389 g]rams to the ultimate adult mass of 3743 g [Wwi = 3743 g]rams represents an approximately ten-fold increase in somatic tissue, a trajectory that demands consistent access to high-quality algal resources on the reef. Gravid individuals nearing this maximum size are often observed foraging intensively on benthic algal turfs, converting primary production into the somatic and gonadal tissues that sustain the population. Long-term monitoring of tagged individuals has confirmed that this asymptotic mass is rarely exceeded, suggesting that metabolic and biomechanical constraints limit further growth even when food is abundant.

The natural lifespan of Acanthurus dussumieri in the wild has been estimated at approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years], derived from otolith-based age validation studies conducted at a mean annual water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. This longevity is remarkable for a reef fish of its body size and reflects a life-history strategy characterised by slow growth, delayed reproduction, and high adult survival. When expressed on a daily basis, the maximum recorded lifespan amounts to roughly 10950 days [am = roughly 10950 days], a duration that allows individuals to accumulate significant reproductive experience over many spawning at a temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] seasons. A gonadosomatic index of approximately 9% [GSI = approximately 9%] was also recorded at 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] in older individuals. Comparative analyses with shorter-lived acanthurids indicate that this extended lifespan is associated with lower natural mortality rates, potentially conferring resilience to moderate levels of exploitation but also rendering the population vulnerable to overfishing if older age classes are preferentially removed.
